title: Localized Thermometry via Dayem Bridges Integrated on Superconducting Qubit Chips
authors: Ella O. Lachman, Dave P. Pappas, Jayss Marshall, Josh Y. Mutus
abstract: Accurate knowledge of the on-chip temperature is essential for understanding and optimizing the performance of superconducting qubits, yet direct thermometry at millikelvin temperatures remains challenging. While qubits themselves are sensitive to the temperature of their environment, other factors may affect the qubits` effective temperature, and using them as thermometers with any accuracy requires specialized measurement protocols and qubit designs, limiting their practicality for routine diagnostics and adding complex infrastructure to any hardware testing apparatus. Here we demonstrate a complementary on-chip thermometry method based on superconducting Dayem bridges that are integrated on the same chip as transmon qubits. By extracting the critical current of the Dayem bridge from I-V measurements, we obtain a local, quantitative measure of the chip temperature without the need for microwave calibration or qubit-specific control sequences. To demonstrate the utility of the Dayem bridges as thermometers, we fabricate them in-situ with qubits on the same chip, calibrate the Dayem bridge critical current as a function of temperature, and characterize its resolution and stability at cryogenic temperatures. We additionally perform simultaneous measurements of the Dayem bridge thermometer and qubit excited-state population, and show agreement over the relevant temperature range, validating the method against established qubit thermometry. Furthermore, we correlate the independently measured chip temperature with qubit energy relaxation and dephasing times, demonstrating the utility of this approach for diagnosing temperature-dependent decoherence mechanisms. These results establish integrated Dayem bridges as a simple, non-invasive, and scalable tool for cryogenic hardware development, and on chip thermometry in superconducting quantum circuits.
summary: The authors present an integrated method using superconducting Dayem Bridges as local thermometers directly on qubit chips. By measuring the temperature dependence of the bridge's critical current, they achieve a simple and non-invasive way to monitor chip temperature at cryogenic levels. This technique successfully validates against standard qubit measurements and proves its utility for diagnosing temperature-dependent decoherence mechanisms in quantum processors.
main_problem: Accurate, localized temperature knowledge is critical for optimizing superconducting qubit performance at millikelvin temperatures.
main_result: The integration of Dayem Bridges (DBs) on the same chip allows for a simple, non-invasive, and scalable measurement of local chip temperature that correlates well with established qubit thermometry methods.
method: Temperature is determined by measuring the superconducting critical current ($I_c$) of an integrated DB bridge via I-V measurements, avoiding complex microwave calibration protocols.
model_or_system: The system involves transmon qubits fabricated on a chip alongside superconducting Dayem Bridges. The thermometry relies on the temperature dependence of $I_c(T)$, which follows the Bardeen relation.
key_observables: Local chip temperature, critical current ($I_c$), qubit energy relaxation times ($T_1$) and dephasing times ($T_2$).
important_parameters: Temperature range from 10 mK to 150 mK; superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$); coherence time decay rates.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that measuring $I_c$ is sufficient to determine the local chip temperature using known material parameters and the Bardeen relation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the co-location of qubits and DBs on a chip, show characteristic $I$-$V$ curves for DBs at different temperatures, and compare qubit coherence times ($T_1$, $T_2$) against inferred temperature from multiple DB thermometers versus the external Mixing Chamber (MXC) temperature.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of on-chip thermometry, details the fabrication and principle of the DB thermometer using $I_c(T)$, validates its readings by comparing them to qubit measurements ($T_{	ext{eff}}$), and finally demonstrates its utility by correlating measured temperature variations with changes in qubit decoherence times.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct, hardware-level diagnostic tool for characterizing the thermal environment of quantum processors, which is crucial input data for theoretical models predicting decoherence sources in solid-state qubits.

Qubit data is presented as box plots, showing the median and the distribution of values. It can be seen that Thermometer 3 is following the MXC temperature as well as the qubits’ effec- tive temperature to lower temperatures than the other two thermometers. This can be attributed to a closer fit of the Ic(0) used in the conversion curve (Fig. 2b) to the actual Ic(0) of the device, and is plausible, as the room-temperature resis- tance of Thermometer 3 deviates from the other thermometer resistances.

FIG. 3. T1 and T2 Ramsey data from 10 qubits (right y-axis) and inferred temperature from 3 DB thermometers (left y-axis) as a function of fridge MXC temperature. Qubit data is presented as box plots, showing the median and the distribution of values. As expected, T1 is less affected by in- creased temperatures than T2 Ramsey. An inverse correlation is observed between the DB-inferred temperature and the T2 Ramsey mean values; this trend confirms the utility of DB thermometers as a proxy for evaluating qubit coherence and dephasing.
